The source wording is difficult. The commentator proposes a corrected reading: if the suited, returning soul has received what it is due, then no new soul should flow from the Giver of Forms. “What it is due” is the object of “receives”; “from among the souls” means some of them; the source of the receiving is the soul itself. The final clause gives the result if that condition holds.
That is, a heavenly body reveals or gives form to familiar images and desires of the soul.

Transmigration does not mean that a soul leaving a body at death moves into another already living body, since then two souls would inhabit one body. It means that a soul moves into matter ready for it, such as an animal embryo in a womb. How could Avicenna allow a human soul to move into a living heavenly body, which already has both an individual soul and a universal intellective soul? Some philosophers did teach a different system: after long ages, the souls of the heavens complete their development and join the intellects; perfected earthly souls rise to take their place, and another group rises later. That system is a form of transmigration.

The claim that a specific readiness fits each soul does not solve the problem. Dust and ash are not ready for a rational human soul. Nature must first bring matter through the perfections of lower kinds before it can rise to a higher kind. Each form requires suitable matter, readiness, and whatever brings about that readiness. Semen cannot receive the form of an embryo until it first takes on the form of a clinging substance; likewise, the matter of an embryo must first pass through its earlier stages. Though matter is what receives each form, the conditions that make it ready are not simply matter itself. Scattered earthly parts could not receive a soul separated from the body without first becoming ready through the forms closer to that soul.

The commentator notes the author's use of a phrase that seems to refer to all pleasures. It is a rhetorical claim, not a sound proof. Removing pain is a kind of absence, and absence cannot itself produce pleasure. The confusion comes from treating something that accompanies pleasure as if it were pleasure itself. Looking at a beautiful face without first being separated from it, hearing a lovely voice, smelling a fragrance, tasting sweetness, or touching a soft body can all be positive pleasures, not relief from pain. God takes joy in His own being, even though religious language about God is carefully defined; He has neither absence nor pain. The same is true of immaterial intellects joined to God.

Both replies are weak. The first does not answer why reward or pain should be given if God is not affected by them. The second assumes the conclusion: if the objection stands, there is no reason for a promise or warning whose truth needs to be shown.

The afterlife soul is self-sufficient and draws everything it chooses from its own inner reality. The one who gives joy and the one who receives it, or the one who causes fear and the one who feels it, are within the same soul; nothing comes from outside to change it. The commentator compares this with the philosophers' account of God's knowledge: it does not affect God, because it does not come from something outside Him. Our knowledge, by contrast, receives forms from outside, through the Active Intellect and the preparation of our awareness.

Worldly things that people grow attached to pass away; those who have not grown close to what lasts will not find it familiar. One might object that their memories of familiar things remain, so they can still enjoy them. The reply gives two reasons they cannot: the horror of the afterlife overwhelms them, and worldly pleasures themselves turn into harm. Wrongfully consuming an orphan's wealth becomes like consuming fire; forbidden food becomes like bitter, poisonous plants. As in the scriptural dream where years of famine and plenty appear as lean and fat cows, a person who devoured orphans' wealth unjustly will perceive themselves as eating fire.

The ordinary, untrained person relies mainly on sense, imagination, and instinct. Without the strength of an example, they would not be reassured. Even if reason were present, without examples suited to it, it would argue with reason and resist understanding abstract realities.

The person in question believed what the Prophet brought, did their best, and sincerely committed to an interpretation. Ghazali also says that the things promised in revelation can exist in five ways: in themselves, intellectually, in imagination, through the senses, or by likeness. Anyone who accepts one of these ways is not to be declared an unbeliever. Only someone who denies all meaning and rejects the promise entirely is an unbeliever.
This includes rules for trade, marriage, inheritance, and related matters.

The commentator says that the verse's phrase “at an appointed time” answers the objection: it names a timeless, eternal day, not a day within ordinary time. A thing in time is not known in itself; it is known through an image that makes it present to awareness. The commentator compares this with the verse, “We send it down only in a measured amount.”

“Returns to God and is gathered to Him” means that the person is annihilated in God and lives through Him: outwardly they have their form in this world, but their inner meaning is with God, where the Hour is known. In their bodily aspect they remain here; in spirit they are in the world beyond nature or in the divine realm. Likewise, their natural body is in time while their spirit is in a higher timeless duration, and their inner meaning is in eternity. Whatever appears there is the form of what exists here; knowledge is the seed of direct vision. The note quotes Persian verses meaning: “Many ask about the Day of Judgment as if they were already there,” and “Whoever has not seen the Beloved's face directly today is like a child waiting for tomorrow.”

“On the face of the earth” can mean the body's ground or the ground of material readiness. It may also mean that as long as someone remains here, there is still a knower and something known, and the Hour has not yet come for them.
This phrase echoes the Qur'anic “in a seat of truth, with a Sovereign who is all-powerful.” The divine presence is a fitting replacement for standing by the body and clinging to the earth.

The commentator lists five meanings of “grave.” First, the body is the grave of the soul, as in the Persian saying, “The souls of the dead are in the grave of the body.” Second, it is the familiar physical grave where the body is buried. Third, it is the imaginal body described in the main text. Fourth, for the soul, it is the set of conditions surrounding it: worldly distractions press in on the soul, sins and ignorance darken it, and knowledge is light. Fifth, for souls free of matter, it is the world of pure intellect. The graves and shrines of these souls are the places the nearest angels visit and surround.

The author answers an objection to spiritual resurrection: if the powers that perceive individual things depend on matter, they perish with the body, while the intellect that survives cannot perceive particulars. He replies that these powers exist in an imaginal, nonmaterial way. They remain with the soul and continue to imagine, understand, and sense particular things.
These forms are shadows of the soul's bright or dark qualities from this life: its good works and knowledge, or the worldly distractions and narrow limits that weighed it down.

The forms of the next life are the same as the imaginal forms of the intermediate state in their basic nature. They differ in strength, weakness, completeness, and attention. In the intermediate state, a person is still turned toward this world; in the next life, this world is forgotten and attention turns fully toward the forms of the afterlife. The intermediate state is like a dream, and this life is like a dream within a dream.

Desire appears as a pig, anger as a wild beast, and deceit as a demon. A person ruled by these natural urges is like someone who serves them and carries out their orders. God says, “Do not worship Satan,” and asks, “Have you seen the one who takes their own desire as their god?”

The reference is to the first level of the power of imagination, which leads back to what philosophers call the material intellect. The account must explain both what remains after death and what is still only a capacity. The author identifies it with imagination because this is the final form reached by the natural powers in this life and the first basis for the forms of the next.
Even if matter and form were only joined together rather than united as one thing, they would still need a shared nature and a close fit. This point does not depend on their being one.

Here, smells and sounds are examples of forms that air receives; the pronouns in the Arabic refer to air. But air does not receive colors, so “lights” may have been intended instead of “colors.” “Rays” does not mean that the material basis for receiving forms is itself a ray; the author's count of three also points to this reading.
Here, “matter” means any underlying basis for something, not only the material that carries an added quality.

The author says that those who notice this will see that imagined and understood forms are more noble, complete, and powerful because their basis is finer. Many people think they are weaker and less important, especially when they treat mental images as mere copies of physical things. If they saw those forms as real in themselves, they would judge the opposite—above all of lasting, universal thoughts free of material coverings and limits.
“Inner causes” here means a person's habits and character traits.

The first verse looks at each person's own place and the preserved core within them. The verses about God's rule look instead at the dropping away of relationships and ranks. Both point to different levels of God's active power: even when created things act, God is the source of their action. All existence is His light and gift; good is in His hand, while evil does not come from Him.

The commentator has already listed several meanings of “grave.” One is the set of habits and deeds, bright or dark, that surround the soul after death. The “grave” and “place of sleep” in the question, “Who woke us from our place of sleep?” are the shadows and forms that enclose the soul between death and Resurrection. These forms grow stronger and more complete as the soul turns away from this world and toward the next, whether in kindness or severity. Resurrection is this waking and full development. The intermediate state is like sleep; resurrection is waking from weak forms and taking on stronger ones.

In reason and in the word's ordinary sense, we are already gathered to God: our existence is hidden and erased beneath His. In the religious sense, this gathering is still to come. It occurs when we leave behind our natural bodies, take on pure forms of the intermediate world, and are gathered through them toward God's expressions of kindness or severity. It is the return of meaning and form to their source.

The commentator explains the seventy-cubit chain through the ties that hold a person back from God. He says that human existence has seven subtle levels, each with ten parts. These are the ten portions from which Adam’s nature was formed: one from the elements and nine from the nine heavenly spheres. Love, for example, is linked to Venus and anger to Mars. The elemental portion at each level refers to earthly qualities and the ability to be affected. In counting the seventy ties, he says to count the final effects and leave out their starting points.

If each of the seventy ties is seen as reflecting a thousand of God’s beautiful names, they make seventy thousand veils of light and darkness, as in a well-known report. Their existence is light, while their limited nature is darkness. For the unhappy, the seventy ties remain only potential and never become a path to God. Even when they become active in a person’s nature and soul, they are like fire if they do not lead to God. Since the person does not see or reflect God’s names, these ties have no living connection with Him; together they form the chain seventy cubits long.

The commentator then gives another way to count these ties. He divides people into seven groups linked to the seven planets: rulers and commanders to the Sun; soldiers to Mars; clerks and accountants to Mercury; scholars and advisers to Jupiter; farmers and people who live in caves or mountains to Saturn; musicians, lovers of adornment, women, and noblewomen to Venus; and travelers and merchants to the Moon. Each group depends on things that support bodily life, such as money. The commentator lists ten kinds of attachment, based on the astrologer’s houses: money; siblings and relatives; property, parents, servants, and animals; children; spouses and partners; young people; misfortunes; people with authority over us; friends; and enemies and large animals. He leaves out the first house because it stands for the self, not an attachment, and the ninth because it stands for knowledge and virtues, which perfect the soul rather than tie it down. Seven groups multiplied by ten attachments make seventy ties that keep the soul from reaching God.

The seventy thousand veils arise because each tie contains a thousand particular concerns. The commentator compares them with the many tasks Adam needed after coming down to earth to obtain even a bite of food, according to a report. Bright veils include family and knowledge when they are not directed toward God; dark veils include money, property, animals, and similar worldly things.

“Their pairs” means a person's habits and the forms those habits take. The Qur'an also uses “pairs” for things joined in different ways: existence and essence, general kind and the feature that sets a kind apart, matter and form, and male and female.
The “wild beasts” include the animal traits that follow from a person's habits. They may also include real animals, though those are gathered only as a secondary part of the event.

This is an animal form without physical matter: the imaginal body, the soul's first bodily link in this life. The life-giving spirit is its second link, and the physical body that covers it is the third.

These inner senses perceive things of the next life. Through them, people trained in spiritual practice perceive what others cannot, as do the prophets. The author earlier cited reports of the Prophet seeing the earth's east and west and hearing the sky groan. A mystic puts it this way: “Beyond these five senses are five more, like pure gold beside copper. The health of these senses comes from a healthy body; the health of those comes as the body fades. Seek the first kind of health from a doctor, and the other from the beloved.”
If a person's habits are good, their forms are smooth-faced and youthful; if their habits are bad, their forms are dark and blue.

Someone might object that images held in imagination cannot perish because they are free of matter, even if they still have size and shape. The author has already shown that imagination and the inward sense that brings together what the outer senses perceive do not depend on matter. The forms of what worldly people love would therefore remain with them, since a thing is what it is because of its form, not its matter. The commentator says this question was answered earlier when the author discussed cause and effect.

“The sun” means the sun of Reality. The world is like a mirage that seems like water but disappears when a person reaches it. A mystic compares worldly people to those who watch the waves and forget the sea, clinging to one wave or bubble even though it will soon break or vanish. Those who turn toward God are like people absorbed in the sea itself. Its greatness keeps them from being distracted by waves and bubbles, except as signs of its works and appearances. The sea is the lasting reality beneath them. The mystic says: “When the court of Truth appears, the traveler who trusted in illusion will be ashamed.”

If someone worships to gain pleasure or escape Hell, they love themselves and turn toward their own reward, not toward God. Early jurists therefore required worship to be directed purely to God. The commentator says this kind of devotion is possible only for those close to God, and cites the saying, “My bliss and My paradise.”

Plato's view should not be read as saying that each personal soul existed earlier in a separate, incomplete form. A higher reality, such as the Active Intellect, exists before the physical world, and the soul exists within it at a higher level: the source contains the branch, and the fuller reality contains its more limited expression. Something is what it is through its fullness, not its lack.

This means perception through the senses of the intermediate and next worlds—in general, perception through the soul's inner images. The author says this can be known through reason and religious reports, and also through direct experience.
The reference is to dreams, spiritual unveilings, sudden glimpses, and similar experiences.

Ibn Arabi seems to mean the natural body. Sadra later says Ibn Arabi relied only on personal experience, which would be impossible if taken literally: it would lead to contradictions, such as the soul's destruction or its moving from one body to another. A thing is itself through its form, and an individual is distinct through the soul and its existence. Ibn Arabi was a religious mystic who guarded Muslim belief, so what he says agrees with the teachings and reports of the faith.

The form is not inside the intermediate world as water is inside a cup. To say a mental form is “in the mind” means it is one level of the mind or soul. In the same way, an outer form is one level of the world outside us.

This means the natural body that has become a corpse: the form seen at the time of questioning. Earlier reports about the soul's long separation from worldly life and its strong turn toward the next life help explain this point.
The questioning itself is one kind of punishment.
This refers to the verse, “On the day the Shin is uncovered and they are called to bow down.”
This refers to a report, quoted earlier in the discussion of al-Ghazali, that paradise has a market where forms are offered.

As explained earlier, a human being can take different forms in the spiritual world, just as jinn can appear in different forms in this world. The commentator alludes to the well-known poem: “My heart has become capable of every form.”

The commentator calls the still-open possibilities of the divine decree “spiritual,” and the settled, merciful commands of God's realm “lordly.” The former still include the possibility of taking different shapes; in the latter, those possibilities have been gathered into a settled outcome.
The Prophet is reported to have said, “Before you there were a thousand thousand worlds and a thousand thousand Adams. Your world is the last of the worlds, and your Adam is the last of the Adams.”

When the Prophet was asked whether he and his followers would also come to the Fire, he replied, “Yes, we passed through it while it was still cool.” They had not fallen into the traps and ties of worldly life. For them, God makes the Fire “cool and safe”; it is like light, not something that burns them or drowns them in its flames.

The two reports do not conflict. “Every child is born with a sound nature” refers to the spirit, which comes from a pure, protected world. “The fortunate person is fortunate in the womb, and the unhappy person is unhappy in the womb” refers to the body's nature and temperament, which may be sound or unsound. The commentator also relates the first report to the bright spirit and the second to the soul's formation in the body's four sources and the way its nature is shaped by good or bad habits. Finally, the first concerns the spirit's pure beginning, while the second concerns what is known from the beginning, in the “Mother of the Book” and the “Mother of Pens,” as in another report: “The fortunate person has been fortunate from eternity, and the unhappy person unhappy from eternity.”

This natural worship means following the commands and limits built into creation, just as religious worship means following God's revealed commands and limits. Both aim to bring a person closer to God. Religious worship also keeps people away from Hell; natural worship draws them away from matter and the lowest levels of nature. Whoever is shaped by spiritual qualities is more open to God's mercy; whoever is ruled by bodily nature moves farther from it. This is why the world is called cursed, along with those who are wholly caught up in it—not those whose bodies are here while their hearts have risen above it. The complete person's simple intellect belongs to the highest, lasting realm, not to time or place, even though their body remains in both. The awake mind knows that references to dates, places, and positions describe only the body's life; the simple intellect is free of them.

The body, as a whole shaped and made one by the soul, does not simply perish. The soul gives it its identity, individuality, and unity. The scattered elements of the body, considered apart from the soul, are not the body itself; they remain much as they were before and after death.

The first statement concerns the soul's original natural power; the second concerns the power it develops over its life. In those who reach full maturity, there is no body in the fullest sense to decay at death. At most, a faint body remains, like a shadow that the soul no longer attends to because it is absorbed in what lies above it.

This refers to God's words: “When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, ‘My Lord, show Yourself to me, so that I may look upon You.’” The soul's “appointed time” is its growth toward a meeting with God over the course of life. God's “speech” is the true speaking of the soul through God, as well as its receiving the levels of practical and theoretical understanding that prepare it to meet Him. God's appearance in the worlds of mercy and power draws out the soul's corresponding qualities. Death is therefore both a natural end and the way to a real meeting with God.

If we set aside the sphere's soul and consider its body alone as matter, little more than a weak extension remains. This extension can be split and broken, like other extended things. As explained earlier, the body of a heavenly sphere is not a separate, strong material thing; its strength comes from the soul that gives it life and movement.

God has placed in the soul a love of lasting life—the life of the Living One who never passes away. This world offers only a borrowed life, mixed with loss and decay. Souls love it because it is a faint reflection of lasting life, and they hate its opposite. But the reality is far greater than its shadow, especially a shadow that has fallen so far from its source.
The goal is for the soul to be gathered in a complete state, not an incomplete one. This requires it to be given enough time to grow.

The answer is contained in the question. Most people do not know that death leads to the life described here. Even if they hear it, it may remain a passing thought rather than firm knowledge. So they still fear death.

The soul is so subtle that it takes on the form of whatever it attends to. At first, it is closely tied to the body and its balanced condition. It is distressed when that balance breaks or the body is torn apart. This is why it feels pain at death, even though its higher nature is not destroyed.

The first purpose—pain and fear that protect the body—applies to ordinary people. The second purpose concerns those who reach the next stage of life. The intermediate world depends on imagination, which everyone has, but its images must become firm. Every being needs time to grow and mature; young children, for example, do not dream in their earliest years. Pain warns of danger before the body is fully formed. Without the ability to feel pain, an animal would lack touch, and without touch it would not be an animal.

A thing must reach its end by changing and becoming something new, as an animal soul on the human path becomes a rational soul, and as reason becomes fully active and acquired. The soul's return to God means that it loses its separate self and is erased in Him. Reaching the final end is another way of describing resurrection and reward. A divine philosopher speaks of this return in both ways: every thing has an end it must reach, including the ends built into nature.

These intellects have a real inner connection because, strictly speaking, they have no separate essence of their own, let alone matter as a separate base. The rules that make things separate from God depend on matter, motion, or what follows from them. None of those apply to the intellects. They belong to the realm of God's own being.
This refers to the question, “For what purpose is it?” The purpose meant here is the final end.

In The Divine Things, the author raises a problem about the principle that the nobler being must come before the lower. It seems there could be another being between God and the First Effect, nobler than that effect but lower than God, and then another between these, without end. This would trap an infinite number of beings between two fixed limits. The author answers that the intellects are like one being with many levels, like one soul with many subtle powers. They are all faces of God and His light, joined to Him in a real, inner connection. There is no actual infinity of separate beings here, only infinitely many ranks within one connected reality.
This proof uses direct awareness. It has two forms: unity with what is known, and the way a cause is present in what it causes. Here, “unity” means losing the separate self in God.

The act of revealing is the same as what is revealed, because the intellect loses its separate self in this account. It has no independent essence; it exists only through its link to God and belongs to God's own realm.

The intellect is not merely like an image in a mirror. It is the image itself, and the mirror is only a comparison. As we have seen, it has no separate essence of its own, so there is no actual mirror here.

The author proves unity in two ways: first, by showing that what is understood in itself is united with the intellect that understands it; second, by showing that knowledge is united with the one who knows.

“It exists through God” means that it depends on Him for its existence. The question “For what cause?” can refer to different causes. Here it means the cause that brings something into being. Earlier, when the author said that a thing's fullness is its end, he meant its purpose. If the text instead reads “standing in God,” that can mean that God gives it existence. This makes it more separate from Him. But if what depends on God is itself not made by another, its connection to God is also not made. The author assumes that these intellects exist necessarily through God, since their necessity and lasting life come from Him.

The author leaves out the souls of the heavenly spheres. Their universal souls are included under rational souls, and their particular souls—the ones spread through the bodies of the spheres—are included under human imaginal souls, since their return follows the same pattern.

A soul reaches a state of purity by gaining the right qualities in this life. The next life is not a place to earn those qualities; it is where what a person has done comes into view. A soul may be drawn toward the Active Intellect by an angel's help, or by the help of a complete human being. The note's phrase “because of the strength of longing” means that the soul longs strongly to be drawn toward it.

Every animal has a form and a meaning: a body and a soul. Each develops through inner change during its life in this world. God gives each being a set time to develop. Once the animal soul has completed that development, it leaves the material body, takes on its imaginal form, and can exist without the natural body. It then joins the other souls of its kind while each remains distinct. The intellect that rules the kind is a broad unity, not a small, countable group; its light is wide enough to hold all their souls and imaginal forms.
We call this a return in its own right. Other kinds of return happen through something else.

This refers to those who say that the soul first arises from the body, then continues after death through inner change, or even before that change. Plato says the soul exists as one in the higher world, not as many separate individuals. Ibn Arabi agrees and calls this shared state the “Presence of Unity.” Others say that the soul exists in this general state at the same time as its separate life in the body. These include some Aristotelians and many religious thinkers who say that the soul is free of matter in its essence but begins with the body.
This is a comparison between the greater world and the smaller world of the human body.

The spirits were not present as separate beings in the unfolding world. They existed together in God's eternal knowledge, distinct there because God's knowledge includes every detail. God's knowledge is complete in one undivided act and at the same time knows everything in detail. The general state means this undivided existence; the detailed state means the many meanings and forms of things, which some call the “fixed essences.”

This applies to written letters if we mean the letters that a natural pen is ready to write. But it does not explain the letters that exist in the universe. Those were hidden in the existence of the Higher Pen, as a poem says: “We were exalted letters, not marks left on the mountain peaks. I am you in knowledge, and you are us; we are all in Him. Ask the one who has arrived.” In God's pure knowledge, I, you, and all things exist together as one, not as separate meanings or essences. Their power comes from the strength and completeness of this unity, and God's power acts through it.

This means the Universal Intellect within the Universal Soul, or the Universal Spirit within the detailed forms. That reading better suits the context. A Persian poem says: “When His power breathed upon the pen, thousands of forms were drawn on the tablet of nonexistence.” Here, “nonexistence” means the essences of forms, which exist only in the mind.
Simple forms are like separate letters; the spirits of compound bodies are like letters joined into words.

A Persian poet says: “I always live in the writer's hand; He keeps me between two fingers. My own being has no movement in it; He moves me at every moment.” The two fingers mean the qualities of beauty and majesty, or gentleness and force.

This follows the reading “forms” instead of “Trumpet.” If read as “Trumpet,” it still fits the author's point. The spiritual blowing and fragrant gift from God is the spirit that joins these forms, as God says, “I breathed into him of My spirit.”

The better view is that the spirits arise from the lower side of the forms, not their higher side. The verse “Then We brought it into a new creation” also suggests that the spirits emerge through a real inner change, not by being made out of material that was already present, as people who look only at physical nature may think.
The “book of the soul” means the soul's inner record, written through its habits and qualities.

In short, there are three views. Two say the soul becomes free of the body's form but still keeps the feature that made it different from other souls. The third says the soul always remains joined to some form, whether in this world, the intermediate world, or the next.

The soul comes before the body in its own nature and in a timeless sense. It gives the body its individual identity. It is also the body's true distinguishing feature, the cause of its special effects. Without a distinguishing feature there can be no kind; without a kind there can be no particular being. We have already shown that a body cannot choose one special form over another for no reason. The body is not first an empty, identical thing that later receives any form. The mistake comes from confusing what exists outside the mind with what we understand in thought.
Ibn Arabi does not deny that the body follows the soul, whether we mean the usual human body or the slow-witted person in the form they take in the intermediate world.

“The same body” means the body whose form makes it the body it is, and whose individual identity comes from its soul and existence. The commentator also wants to protect religious teaching and the beliefs of ordinary Muslims. As the author has said, the well-known teaching is that on the Day of Resurrection this is the same body and the same soul. The difference lies in the qualities of each state: worldly, intermediate, or next-life.

The plant has something like touch-awareness. If it truly had the sense of touch, it would be an animal, since touch distinguishes animals. It would also move by its own choice. But nature rises from lower to higher in order, so the plant cannot have full touch-awareness.
God gives the plant a set time to develop its form and soul. The author wrote earlier about particular animal souls in a way that also applies here.

These trees are not separate from the heavenly trees; they are contained within them. They also include trees formed from human habits and actions. In paradise, the ground is ready for planting, and its plants are words of praise to God.

The Lote Tree is described in Qur'anic commentary as standing to the right of the Throne, above the seventh heaven. The knowledge of every angel ends there, and what rises to heaven or descends from above passes through it. The tree is covered by what covers it. The commentator reads it as the Great Intermediate World, the end of the journey of perfected souls and their actions and knowledge, and the highest level of God's names. Angels gathering around it like ravens means that those who travel toward God reach their end there. There is no village beyond Abadan. On this reading, the Lote Tree means a blessed state of wonder, as in the Prophet's prayer, “Lord, increase me in wonder of You,” and Ibn al-Farid's line: “I think the limit of waking and drunkenness is my ascent toward her; my home lies at the farthest point of the Lote Tree.” The word for the tree is also linked to an illness of the head called sudar.

I repeat this point because the evidence that existence is the same as these qualities, and that their levels follow the levels of existence, can be seen by looking at the human soul. This is even clearer when we look at intellect and what lies above it. The soul is knowledge, will, and love through its very being. Its being is at once awareness of itself and its powers, present knowledge of itself, life, light, and the ability to act through all its powers. The same is true, even more fully, of intellect and what lies above it. In extended bodies, however, completeness in every quality is also a lack in every quality.

The author does not mean that the forms that flow into matter are themselves gathered after death, since they belong to this worldly life. He means that they are gathered in the same way as simple beings are.

The difference from the first principle is only what blocks the form from rising higher. At the first level, the obstacles are distance in space, duration in time, and darkness of matter. At the later level, the obstacle is conflict between forms. What brings the forms together also differs: at first, existence itself; later, balance and a well-ordered mixture.
These are imaginal forms, also called suspended images.
